content: 1. Patients with severe anaemia living in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission should receive a full therapeutic course of antimalarial medication at predetermined intervals after being discharged from the hospital. This approach aims to reduce the risk of re-admission and mortality. 2. Post-discharge malaria chemoprevention (PDMC) is recommended for children admitted with severe anaemia not caused by blood loss due to trauma, surgery, malignancy, or bleeding disorders. The implementation of PDMC should be tailored to the specific needs of children with severe anaemia, considering the duration of protection provided by the selected antimalarial drug and the feasibility and affordability of delivering additional PDMC courses. 3. Moderate to high perennial malaria transmission settings are defined as areas where the prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum parasites exceeds 10% or the annual parasite incidence is greater than 250 cases per 1,000 population. These thresholds are indicative and should not be considered absolute for determining the applicability of PDMC recommendations. 4. Mass drug administration (MDA) with antimalarial medicines can be used in areas with moderate to high P. falciparum transmission to achieve short-term reductions in disease burden. However, the effect of MDA wanes within 1–3 months. If implemented, MDA should be part of a comprehensive malaria control program that includes effective case management and appropriate prevention tools and strategies. 5. Malaria programs should assess the suitability of MDA based on the desired impact, level of endemicity, and available resources. MDA for burden reduction should target moderate to high transmission settings, regardless of seasonality. 6. In emergency settings or during disruptions to health services, MDA can be used in defined geographical areas to provide short-term reductions in the burden of P. falciparum malaria. However, evidence on the impact of MDA in emergency settings is limited, and its effects will vary depending on the type of emergency, health service disruption, transmission intensity, drug choice, and delivery method. 7. In areas with very low to low P. falciparum transmission, MDA can be used as chemoprevention to reduce transmission. However, the effect wanes within 1–3 months. MDA should be part of a robust malaria elimination program to minimize the risk of resurgence after the intervention ends. 8. MDA for P. vivax transmission reduction may be considered in areas with P. vivax transmission. However, the effect wanes within 1–3 months. MDA should be part of a comprehensive malaria elimination program that includes treatment for hypnozoites and appropriate prevention strategies. 9. Mass relapse prevention (MRP) using an 8-aminoquinoline medicine alone to reduce P. vivax transmission is not recommended due to the potential for severe harm in individuals with G6PD deficiency. G6PD testing for large populations would significantly increase the complexity and cost of the intervention. 10. The RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine is recommended for the prevention of P. falciparum malaria in children living in regions with moderate to high transmission. It should be administered in a four-dose schedule starting at 5 months of age. In areas with highly seasonal malaria, a five-dose seasonal strategy may be considered. 11. All suspected malaria cases should be confirmed with a parasitological test, either microscopy or rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Both methods should be supported by a quality assurance program. 12. Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are recommended for treating uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in children and adults. The recommended ACTs include artemether-lumefantrine, artesunate-amodiaquine, artesunate-mefloquine, dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine, artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine, and artesunate-pyronaridine. However, some ACTs are contraindicated during the first trimester of pregnancy. 13. Pregnant women with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria in the first trimester should be treated with artemether-lumefantrine. Other ACTs may be considered if artemether-lumefantrine is unavailable, but antifolates and ACTs containing sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine are contraindicated during the first trimester. 14. Infants weighing less than 5 kg with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with ACTs at the same mg/kg body weight target dose as children weighing 5 kg or more. 15. In individuals co-infected with HIV and P. falciparum malaria, artesunate + sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine is not recommended if they are receiving co-trimoxazole, and artesunate + amodiaquine is not recommended if they are receiving efavirenz or zidovudine. 16. Non-immune travelers returning to non-endemic settings with uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria should be treated with an ACT. 17. People with uncomplicated hyperparasitaemia caused by P. falciparum should receive appropriate treatment to reduce the risk of severe disease progression.
